title: Στέντωρ
titleEn: Hera and Athena Go Down to the Fight — Iliad 5.719–813
part: Hera and Athena Go Down to the Fight (5.719–813)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hera and Hebe fit out the chariot, and Athena lays aside her robe and arms herself with the aegis, the helmet and the heavy spear. The two drive through the gates of heaven, which open of themselves, to Zeus on the peak of Olympus, and Hera asks whether he will mind if she drives Ares from the battle; Zeus tells her to send Athena against him. They fly down to where the Simois and the Scamander meet, and Hera sets the horses free to graze on ambrosia in a mist. In the likeness of bronze-voiced Stentor she shames the Argives: while Achilles fought, the Trojans never came out in front of their gates. Athena finds Diomedes cooling his wound by his chariot and rebukes him: Tydeus, small in build but a fighter, would not have held back, so either weariness or fear must have sunk into his son.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse thea glaukōpis Athēnē.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and did not disobey, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: So Hera spoke, and the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, did not disobey.
sentences.n: Athena does as Hera has just asked; Hera’s speech ended at 5.718. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so she spoke’ (ἔφατ’ is the elided middle imperfect of φημί), and οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ‘and did not disobey’ is a formula for ready obedience. Ἀθήνη is named with her stock epithet γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ (the old explanation is ‘owl-eyed’; the sense is not certain). The line is the same as 2.166, where Athena also obeys Hera, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἐποιχομένη χρυσάμπυκας ἔντυεν ἵππους
Ἥρη πρέσβα θεὰ θυγάτηρ μεγάλοιο Κρόνοιο·
sentences.tr:
hē men epoichomenē chrysampykas entyen hippous
Hērē presba thea thygatēr megaloio Kronoio·
sentences.l:
She, on the one hand, going to and fro, was making ready the gold-frontleted horses,
Hera, eldest goddess, daughter of great Cronus;
sentences.i: Hera, the eldest goddess, daughter of great Cronus, went about making ready the horses with their golden frontlets;
sentences.n: The two goddesses now get the chariot ready, and the work is shared out: ἣ μὲν ‘she, on the one hand’ is answered by Ἥβη δ’ ‘and Hebe’ in the next line. ἐποιχομένη ‘going to and fro’ is the present participle of ἐποίχομαι, and ἔντυεν ‘was making ready’ the imperfect of ἐντύω (also ἐντύνω) ‘fit out’. χρυσάμπυκας ‘gold-frontleted’ belongs to the horses (an ἄμπυξ is a band worn on the brow). The second line names the subject: πρέσβα ‘eldest’ is also a title of honour, and Hera does call herself the eldest child of Cronus at 4.59; Κρόνοιο is the epic genitive in -οιο (= -ου).

sentences.t:
Ἥβη δ’ ἀμφ’ ὀχέεσσι θοῶς βάλε καμπύλα κύκλα
χάλκεα ὀκτάκνημα σιδηρέῳ ἄξονι ἀμφίς.
sentences.tr:
Hēbē d’ amph’ ocheessi thoōs bale kampyla kykla
chalkea oktaknēma sidēreōi axoni amphis.
sentences.l:
And Hebe swiftly put about the chariot the bent wheels,
bronze, eight-spoked, on the iron axle, on both sides.
sentences.i: And Hebe quickly fitted the bent wheels to the chariot, bronze wheels with eight spokes, one on each side of the iron axle.
sentences.n: Hebe fits the wheels. ἀμφί … βάλε ‘put round’ is split by tmesis, and ὀχέεσσι is the epic dative plural of ὄχος ‘carriage’, the plural standing for one chariot (as ὄχεα does at 745). καμπύλα κύκλα are ‘bent wheels’, wheels with curved rims; κύκλα is the Homeric plural of κύκλος ‘circle, wheel’. ὀκτάκνημα ‘eight-spoked’ uses κνήμη, which is ‘shin’ and, of a wheel, ‘spoke’. σιδηρέῳ is the uncontracted epic form of σιδηρῷ ‘iron’, and ἀμφίς ‘on both sides’ goes with ἄξονι ‘axle’.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἤτοι χρυσέη ἴτυς ἄφθιτος, αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε
χάλκε’ ἐπίσσωτρα προσαρηρότα, θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
tōn ētoi chryseē itys aphthitos, autar hyperthe
chalke’ epissōtra prosarērota, thauma idesthai·
sentences.l:
Of these the rim is golden, unfailing, and above it
bronze tires are fitted on, a wonder to see;
sentences.i: Their rim is of gold, unfailing, and over it are fitted tires of bronze, a wonder to behold;
sentences.n: The description of the wheels goes on, with ‘is’ understood in both clauses. τῶν ‘of these’ points back to the wheels. ἴτυς is the rim, here χρυσέη ‘golden’ (epic uncontracted, = χρυσῆ) and ἄφθιτος ‘unfailing’, said of what does not decay. The ἐπίσσωτρα ‘tires’ are the bands laid over the rim, and προσαρηρότα is the neuter plural perfect participle of προσαραρίσκω ‘fit on’. θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι ‘a wonder to see’ (ἰδέσθαι is an aorist infinitive) is a stock phrase.

sentences.t: πλῆμναι δ’ ἀργύρου εἰσὶ περίδρομοι ἀμφοτέρωθεν·
sentences.tr: plēmnai d’ argyrou eisi peridromoi amphoterōthen·
sentences.l: and the naves are of silver, running round on both sides;
sentences.i: and the hubs are made of silver, running round on either side;
sentences.n: πλῆμναι are the ‘naves’, the hubs at the centre of the wheels. ἀργύρου ‘of silver’ is a genitive of material, with εἰσί ‘are’, and περίδρομοι ‘running round’ (περί ‘round’ + δρόμος ‘run’) says how the silver is set; the poet does not say more, and the sense is not clear. The same word is used of the rails at 728. ἀμφοτέρωθεν is ‘on both sides’ (ἀμφότερος ‘both’ + the suffix -θεν).

sentences.t:
δίφρος δὲ χρυσέοισι καὶ ἀργυρέοισιν ἱμᾶσιν
ἐντέταται, δοιαὶ δὲ περίδρομοι ἄντυγές εἰσι.
sentences.tr:
diphros de chryseoisi kai argyreoisin himasin
entetatai, doiai de peridromoi antyges eisi.
sentences.l:
and the chariot-board with gold and silver straps
is strung, and two rails running round are on it.
sentences.i: The chariot-board is strung with straps of gold and silver, and there are two rails running round it.
sentences.n: δίφρος is the ‘chariot-board’, the floor of the car on which the driver stands. ἱμᾶσιν ‘with straps’ is the dative plural of ἱμάς ‘strap’, with the epic datives χρυσέοισι and ἀργυρέοισιν ‘golden and silver’, and ἐντέταται is the perfect passive of ἐντείνω ‘stretch in’, so the board is strung with straps. δοιαί ‘two’ is the epic form of δύο, and ἄντυγες, plural of ἄντυξ, are the ‘rails’ of the car (the rail to which the reins are made fast, 5.262).

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ἐξ ἀργύρεος ῥυμὸς πέλεν·
sentences.tr: tou d’ ex argyreos rhymos pelen·
sentences.l: and out from it was a silver pole;
sentences.i: and a silver pole came out from it;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘it’ points back to the chariot-board. ἐξ … πέλεν is ‘was out from’, with πέλεν the unaugmented imperfect of πέλω ‘be’. ῥυμός is the ‘pole’, the shaft that runs forward from the car, and ἀργύρεος ‘silver’ is the epic form in -εος (= ἀργυροῦς).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ ἄκρῳ
δῆσε χρύσειον καλὸν ζυγόν, ἐν δὲ λέπαδνα
κάλ’ ἔβαλε χρύσει’·
sentences.tr:
autar ep’ akrōi
dēse chryseion kalon zygon, en de lepadna
kal’ ebale chrysei’·
sentences.i: and at the tip of it she tied a fair golden yoke, and laid golden yoke-straps, fine ones, upon it;
sentences.n: ἐπ’ ἄκρῳ ‘at the tip’ is the end of the pole. The unnamed subject of δῆσε ‘bound’ (unaugmented, = ἔδησε) and ἔβαλε ‘laid’ is still Hebe, who has been fitting the car; Hera comes back as subject in the next line. ἐν … ἔβαλε is split by tmesis. λέπαδνα are the ‘yoke-straps’, the straps that go with the yoke; the exact fitting is not clear. κάλ’ and χρύσει’ are the elided καλά and χρύσεια, neuter plural, ‘fine’ and ‘golden’, agreeing with λέπαδνα.

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δὲ ζυγὸν ἤγαγεν Ἥρη
ἵππους ὠκύποδας, μεμαυῖ’ ἔριδος καὶ ἀϋτῆς.
sentences.tr:
hypo de zygon ēgagen Hērē
hippous ōkypodas, memaui’ eridos kai aÿtēs.
sentences.l:
and under the yoke Hera led
the swift-footed horses, eager for strife and the battle-cry.
sentences.i: and Hera led the swift-footed horses under the yoke, eager for strife and the battle-cry.
sentences.n: ὑπὸ … ἤγαγεν is ‘led under’ (the yoke), with Ἥρη as subject. ὠκύποδας ‘swift-footed’ is the epithet of the horses. μεμαυῖ’ is the elided feminine participle μεμαυῖα ‘eager’, agreeing with Ἥρη and not with the masculine ἵππους, so it is Hera who is eager; it takes the genitives ἔριδος καὶ ἀϋτῆς ‘for strife and the battle-cry’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
πέπλον μὲν κατέχευεν ἑανὸν πατρὸς ἐπ’ οὔδει
ποικίλον, ὅν ῥ’ αὐτὴ ποιήσατο καὶ κάμε χερσίν·
sentences.tr:
autar Athēnaiē kourē Dios aigiochoio
peplon men katecheuen heanon patros ep’ oudei
poikilon, hon rh’ autē poiēsato kai kame chersin·
sentences.i: But Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, let fall on her father’s floor the fine robe, the intricate one, which she herself had made and toiled at with her hands;
sentences.n: The scene turns to Athena. αὐτὰρ ‘but’ marks the turn, and the μέν of πέπλον μὲν is answered by ἣ δὲ at 736. Ἀθηναίη κούρη Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is ‘Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus’ (κούρη ‘girl, daughter’; epic genitive -οιο). κατέχευεν is ‘poured down’, i.e. let fall, and πατρὸς ἐπ’ οὔδει is ‘on her father’s floor’. ἑανόν ‘fine’ is uncertain in sense (perhaps ‘soft’ or ‘light’), and ποικίλον ‘intricate’ means worked with a pattern. ὅν ῥ’ = ὅν ῥα ‘which’; ποιήσατο is the aorist middle ‘made for herself’, and κάμε the unaugmented aorist of κάμνω ‘toil’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ χιτῶν’ ἐνδῦσα Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο
τεύχεσιν ἐς πόλεμον θωρήσσετο δακρυόεντα.
sentences.tr:
hē de chitōn’ endysa Dios nephelēgeretao
teuchesin es polemon thōrēsseto dakryoenta.
sentences.l:
and she, having put on the tunic of cloud-gatherer Zeus,
with arms armed herself for war, tearful.
sentences.i: and she put on the tunic of Zeus who gathers the clouds and armed herself with weapons for tearful war.
sentences.n: ἣ δὲ ‘and she’ answers the πέπλον μέν of 734: she lays the robe aside and puts on a tunic that belongs to Zeus. χιτῶν’ is the elided accusative χιτῶνα ‘tunic’, and ἐνδῦσα the aorist participle of ἐνδύω ‘put on’; Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο ‘of cloud-gatherer Zeus’ says whose tunic it is. τεύχεσιν is the dative plural ‘with arms’, and θωρήσσετο ‘armed herself’ the imperfect middle. δακρυόεντα ‘tearful’ agrees with πόλεμον ‘war’, the war that brings tears.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ὤμοισιν βάλετ’ αἰγίδα θυσσανόεσσαν
δεινήν, ἣν περὶ μὲν πάντῃ Φόβος ἐστεφάνωται,
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ ōmoisin balet’ aigida thyssanoessan
deinēn, hēn peri men pantēi Phobos estephanōtai,
sentences.l:
And about her shoulders she threw the tasselled aegis,
dread, around which on every side Terror is wreathed,
sentences.i: About her shoulders she threw the tasselled aegis, dread, with Terror wreathed round it on every side,
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … βάλετ’ is ‘threw round’ (tmesis; βάλετ’ is the elided aorist middle βάλετο), and ὤμοισιν ‘about her shoulders’ is a dative of place. αἰγίδα is the aegis, a goatskin storm-shield with tassels, here worn by Athena, and θυσσανόεσσαν is ‘tasselled’ (from θύσανος ‘tassel’). In ἣν περὶ … ἐστεφάνωται the περί follows its relative pronoun: ‘around which Terror is wreathed’, ἐστεφάνωται being the perfect passive of στεφανόω, and Φόβος ‘Terror’ is a personified figure set round the shield. πάντῃ is ‘on every side’.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ Ἔρις, ἐν δ’ Ἀλκή, ἐν δὲ κρυόεσσα Ἰωκή,
sentences.tr: en d’ Eris, en d’ Alkē, en de kryoessa Iōkē,
sentences.l: and on it Strife, and on it Might, and on it chilling Onset,
sentences.i: and on it Strife, and Might, and chilling Onset,
sentences.n: The figures on the aegis are listed with ἐν δ’ ‘and on it’ and no verb. Ἔρις is ‘Strife’ and Ἀλκή ‘Might’, both personified. Ἰωκή ‘Onset’ is the rush of battle (the plural ἰωκάς occurs at 5.521); the exact sense is not certain. κρυόεσσα ‘chilling’ is the feminine of κρυόεις, from κρύος ‘chill, frost’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ τε Γοργείη κεφαλὴ δεινοῖο πελώρου
δεινή τε σμερδνή τε, Διὸς τέρας αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
en de te Gorgeiē kephalē deinoio pelōrou
deinē te smerdnē te, Dios teras aigiochoio.
sentences.l:
and on it the Gorgon head of a dread monster,
dread and frightful, a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.i: and on it the Gorgon head of a dread monster, dread and frightful, a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.n: The last figure is the Gorgon’s head. Γοργείη is the adjective ‘of the Gorgon’, agreeing with κεφαλή, and δεινοῖο πελώρου ‘of a dread monster’ is the epic genitive in -οιο; the same words stand at Odyssey 11.634, and the English is kept. δεινή τε σμερδνή τε is ‘dread and frightful’, and Διὸς τέρας αἰγιόχοιο is ‘a portent of aegis-bearing Zeus’, in apposition to the head (τέρας ‘portent, sign’).

sentences.t:
κρατὶ δ’ ἐπ’ ἀμφίφαλον κυνέην θέτο τετραφάληρον
χρυσείην, ἑκατὸν πολίων πρυλέεσσ’ ἀραρυῖαν·
sentences.tr:
krati d’ ep’ amphiphalon kyneēn theto tetraphalēron
chryseiēn, hekaton poliōn pryleess’ araruian·
sentences.l:
And on her head she set the two-ridged helmet, four-ridged,
golden, fitted for the foot-soldiers of a hundred cities;
sentences.i: On her head she set the helmet, two-ridged and four-ridged, golden, fitted for the foot-soldiers of a hundred cities;
sentences.n: κρατὶ … ἐπὶ … θέτο is ‘set on her head’ (tmesis, θέτο the unaugmented aorist middle of τίθημι), and κυνέην is the epic accusative ‘helmet’. ἀμφίφαλον and τετραφάληρον are built on φάλος, which is usually taken as the ridge of the helmet (3.362); ‘two-ridged’ and ‘four-ridged’ are the literal readings, and what the helmet looked like is not known. ἀραρυῖαν, the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω, is ‘fitted’, agreeing with κυνέην; ἑκατὸν πολίων πρυλέεσσ’ is ‘for the foot-soldiers of a hundred cities’, and whether the helmet is meant to suit them, or to carry their figures, the Greek does not say.

sentences.t:
ἐς δ’ ὄχεα φλόγεα ποσὶ βήσετο, λάζετο δ’ ἔγχος
βριθὺ μέγα στιβαρόν, τῷ δάμνησι στίχας ἀνδρῶν
ἡρώων, οἷσίν τε κοτέσσεται ὀβριμοπάτρη.
sentences.tr:
es d’ ochea phlogea posi bēseto, lazeto d’ enchos
brithy mega stibaron, tōi damnēsi stichas andrōn
hērōōn, hoisin te kotessetai obrimopatrē.
sentences.l:
and onto the chariot, flaming, with her feet she stepped, and took up a spear
heavy, huge, massive, with which she overpowers the ranks of men,
of heroes, with whomever she is angered, she of the mighty father.
sentences.i: She stepped with her feet into the flaming chariot and took up a spear, heavy and huge and massive, with which she beats down the ranks of men, of heroes, with whomever she, the daughter of a mighty father, is angered.
sentences.n: ἐς … βήσετο is ‘stepped into’ (an epic mixed aorist, unaugmented), and ὄχεα, the plural for one chariot, is called φλόγεα ‘flaming’ (from φλόξ ‘flame’; the poet does not say whether it shines or burns). The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of φλόγεα, short by nature, has to be counted long, in the third foot. λάζετο is ‘took hold of’. The last two lines are the Odyssey’s description of the same spear (Odyssey 1.100–101), and its English is kept: τῷ ‘with which’, δάμνησι ‘overpowers’ (epic -ησι), στίχας ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων ‘the ranks of men, of heroes’, and οἷσίν τε κοτέσσεται ‘with whomever she is angered’ (the Odyssey has τοῖσίν here). ὀβριμοπάτρη ‘she of the mighty father’ is an epithet of Athena alone.

sentences.t: Ἥρη δὲ μάστιγι θοῶς ἐπεμαίετ’ ἄρ’ ἵππους·
sentences.tr: Hērē de mastigi thoōs epemaiet’ ar’ hippous·
sentences.l: And Hera swiftly with the whip reached out at the horses;
sentences.i: And Hera quickly laid the whip to the horses;
sentences.n: Hera now drives. μάστιγι is the instrumental dative ‘with the whip’, and θοῶς ‘swiftly’ the adverb of θοός. ἐπεμαίετ’ is the elided imperfect middle of ἐπιμαίομαι ‘reach at, touch’, which with a whip means to lay it on; ἄρ’ is the particle ἄρα ‘then’.

sentences.t: αὐτόμαται δὲ πύλαι μύκον οὐρανοῦ ἃς ἔχον Ὧραι,
sentences.tr: automatai de pylai mykon ouranou has echon Hōrai,
sentences.l: And of themselves the gates of heaven bellowed, which the Hours kept,
sentences.i: Then of their own accord the gates of heaven, which the Hours kept, bellowed;
sentences.n: The gates of heaven open for the chariot. αὐτόμαται ‘of themselves’ is the nominative plural feminine, agreeing with πύλαι ‘gates’, and οὐρανοῦ is the genitive ‘of heaven’. μύκον ‘bellowed’ is a past tense without the augment of μυκάομαι ‘low, bellow’, the sound that cattle make. ἃς ἔχον Ὧραι is ‘which the Hours kept’: the Ὧραι ‘Hours’ are goddesses who guard the gates.

sentences.t:
τῇς ἐπιτέτραπται μέγας οὐρανὸς Οὔλυμπός τε
ἠμὲν ἀνακλῖναι πυκινὸν νέφος ἠδ’ ἐπιθεῖναι.
sentences.tr:
tēis epitetraptai megas ouranos Oulympos te
ēmen anaklinai pykinon nephos ēd’ epitheinai.
sentences.l:
to whom are entrusted great heaven and Olympus,
both to open and to shut the solid cloud.
sentences.i: Great heaven and Olympus are in their charge, both to open and to shut the solid cloud.
sentences.n: τῇς is the epic dative plural of the relative, ‘to whom’, referring to the Hours, and ἐπιτέτραπται is the perfect passive of ἐπιτρέπω ‘entrust’, with μέγας οὐρανὸς Οὔλυμπός τε ‘great heaven and Olympus’ as the things entrusted. ἠμὲν … ἠδ’ is ‘both … and’. ἀνακλῖναι ‘to lay back’ and ἐπιθεῖναι ‘to put on’ are aorist infinitives, and since the cloud works like a door, the English gives their sense, ‘to open’ and ‘to shut’, as at Odyssey 11.525, where the same words are said of the ambush. πυκινόν ‘solid’ is the house word for πυκινός.

sentences.t: τῇ ῥα δι’ αὐτάων κεντρηνεκέας ἔχον ἵππους·
sentences.tr: tēi rha di’ autaōn kentrēnekeas echon hippous·
sentences.l: That way, through them, the goad-driven horses they drove;
sentences.i: Through these gates they drove their goad-driven horses;
sentences.n: τῇ ‘that way’ and δι’ αὐτάων ‘through them’ refer to the gates; αὐτάων is the epic genitive plural feminine of αὐτός. ἔχον is ‘drove’ (as at 3.263), and its plural shows that both goddesses are in the car. κεντρηνεκέας is built on κέντρον ‘goad’ and a root meaning ‘carry’, and is usually taken to mean ‘driven on by the goad’; the exact sense is not known.

sentences.t:
εὗρον δὲ Κρονίωνα θεῶν ἄτερ ἥμενον ἄλλων
ἀκροτάτῃ κορυφῇ πολυδειράδος Οὐλύμποιο.
sentences.tr:
heuron de Kroniōna theōn ater hēmenon allōn
akrotatēi koryphēi polydeirados Oulympoio.
sentences.l:
and they found the son of Cronus sitting apart from the other gods
on the topmost peak of many-ridged Olympus.
sentences.i: They found the son of Cronus sitting apart from the other gods on the topmost peak of many-ridged Olympus.
sentences.n: εὗρον ‘they found’ has the two goddesses as subject. Κρονίωνα ‘the son of Cronus’ is Zeus, not named, and θεῶν ἄτερ … ἄλλων is ‘apart from the other gods’, with ἥμενον ‘sitting’. Line 754 is the same as 1.499, where Thetis finds Zeus: ἀκροτάτῃ is the superlative ‘topmost’, πολυδειράδος ‘many-ridged’ (δειράς ‘ridge’), and Οὐλύμποιο the epic genitive. Its English is kept; 753 differs from 1.498 in verb and epithet.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἵππους στήσασα θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη
Ζῆν’ ὕπατον Κρονίδην ἐξείρετο καὶ προσέειπε·
sentences.tr:
enth’ hippous stēsasa thea leukōlenos Hērē
Zēn’ hypaton Kronidēn exeireto kai proseeipe·
sentences.l:
There, having stopped the horses, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
Zeus, highest son-of-Cronus, questioned and addressed:
sentences.i: There white-armed Hera, the goddess, stopped her horses and questioned Zeus, the son of Cronus, the highest one, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ‘there’ and στήσασα ‘having stopped’ (aorist participle of ἵστημι, transitive) set the scene, and λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is Hera’s stock epithet. Ζῆν’ is the elided accusative Ζῆνα ‘Zeus’, with ὕπατον ‘highest’ and Κρονίδην ‘son of Cronus’. ἐξείρετο is the imperfect of ἐξείρομαι ‘ask out, question’, here with the accusative of the person, and προσέειπε ‘addressed’ is the aorist of προσεῖπον.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ οὐ νεμεσίζῃ Ἄρῃ τάδε καρτερὰ ἔργα
ὁσσάτιόν τε καὶ οἷον ἀπώλεσε λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν
μὰψ ἀτὰρ οὐ κατὰ κόσμον ἐμοὶ δ’ ἄχος, οἳ δὲ ἕκηλοι
τέρπονται Κύπρίς τε καὶ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
ἄφρονα τοῦτον ἀνέντες, ὃς οὔ τινα οἶδε θέμιστα;
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater ou nemesizēi Arēi tade kartera erga
hossation te kai hoion apōlese laon Achaiōn
maps atar ou kata kosmon emoi d’ achos, hoi de hekēloi
terpontai Kypris te kai argyrotoxos Apollōn
aphrona touton anentes, hos ou tina oide themista;
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, do you not feel resentment at Ares for these mighty deeds,
how great and of what sort a host of the Achaeans he has destroyed,
recklessly and not in due order, and to me is grief, while they at ease
take delight, Cypris and silver-bowed Apollo,
having let go this senseless one, who knows no rules of right?
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, do you not feel resentment at Ares for these mighty deeds, how great a host of the Achaeans, and what a host, he has destroyed, recklessly and not in due order, and the grief is mine, while they take delight at their ease, Cypris and silver-bowed Apollo, who have let this senseless creature loose, who knows no rules of right?
sentences.n: Hera’s speech is one long question. ζεῦ πάτερ ‘father Zeus’ is a vocative; οὐ νεμεσίζῃ is ‘do you not feel resentment’, taking the dative Ἄρῃ ‘at Ares’, with τάδε καρτερὰ ἔργα ‘these mighty deeds’ as the cause. ὁσσάτιον τε καὶ οἷον ‘how great and of what sort’ agree with λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν ‘a host of the Achaeans’, and ἀπώλεσε is the aorist ‘has destroyed’; μάψ ‘recklessly’ and οὐ κατὰ κόσμον ‘not in due order’ give the manner. ἐμοὶ δ’ ἄχος is ‘and to me is grief’, with no verb. The subjects of τέρπονται ‘take delight’ are Κύπρις, Aphrodite, and Apollo, and ἕκηλοι ‘at ease’ agrees with them. ἀνέντες is the aorist participle of ἀνίημι ‘let loose’, masculine plural because Apollo is one of the two, and ἄφρονα τοῦτον ‘this senseless one’ is Ares. θέμιστα is ‘rules of right’, plural of θέμις ‘custom, right’. The question that began at 757 ends here.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ἦ ῥά τί μοι κεχολώσεαι, αἴ κεν Ἄρηα
λυγρῶς πεπληγυῖα μάχης ἐξαποδίωμαι;
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater ē rha ti moi kecholōseai, ai ken Arēa
lygrōs peplēguia machēs exapodiōmai;
sentences.l:
Father Zeus, can it be that you will be at all angry with me, if Ares
grievously having struck I drive out of the battle?”
sentences.i: Father Zeus, will you be at all angry with me if I strike Ares a grievous blow and drive him out of the battle?”
sentences.n: A second question, this one the real request. ἦ ῥά introduces it, and τί μοι κεχολώσεαι is ‘will you be angry with me at all’ (κεχολώσεαι the future perfect of χολόομαι, with epic -εαι for -ῃ). αἴ κεν … ἐξαποδίωμαι is ‘if I drive out’, a subjunctive with κεν in a condition. Ἄρηα is the object of both verbs, with πεπληγυῖα ‘having struck’, the feminine perfect participle of πλήσσω, taking an aorist sense, and λυγρῶς ‘grievously’ going with it. μάχης is a genitive of separation, ‘out of the battle’.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: Zeus replies. The line is the same as 1.560 and its English is kept: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘her answering’, προσέφη ‘addressed’, and νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’, with the epic nominative in -τα for -της.

sentences.t:
ἄγρει μάν οἱ ἔπορσον Ἀθηναίην ἀγελείην,
ἥ ἑ μάλιστ’ εἴωθε κακῇς ὀδύνῃσι πελάζειν.
sentences.tr:
agrei man hoi eporson Athēnaiēn ageleiēn,
hē he malist’ eiōthe kakēis odynēisi pelazein.
sentences.l:
“Come then, set Athena the spoil-driver on him,
who is most accustomed to bring him near to grievous pains.”
sentences.i: “Come, then, rouse Athena, the driver of spoil, against him; she is the one most accustomed to bring him near to grievous pains.”
sentences.n: Zeus gives his leave in two lines. ἄγρει μάν is ‘come now’, and ἔπορσον is an order, ‘rouse against’ (from ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ with ἐπί), with οἱ ‘him’, Ares, as the dative of the person. Ἀθηναίην ἀγελείην is ‘Athena the spoil-driver’; ἀγελείη is probably ἄγω ‘drive’ + λεία ‘spoil’, and the sense is not certain. In ἥ ἑ μάλιστ’ εἴωθε the pronoun ἑ is ‘him’ (Ares), εἴωθε is the perfect ‘is accustomed’, and κακῇς ὀδύνῃσι is the epic dative plural ‘to grievous pains’, after πελάζειν ‘to bring near’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
μάστιξεν δ’ ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse thea leukōlenos Hērē,
mastixen d’ hippous·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and did not disobey, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
and she whipped the horses;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the goddess, white-armed Hera, did not disobey; she whipped the horses;
sentences.n: The line is the formula of 5.719, now with Hera obeying Zeus. μάστιξεν is the aorist ‘whipped’, unaugmented (= ἐμάστιξεν), with ν-movable, and it takes the accusative ἵππους directly.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην
μεσσηγὺς γαίης τε καὶ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος.
sentences.tr:
tō d’ ouk aekonte petesthēn
messēgys gaiēs te kai ouranou asteroentos.
sentences.l:
and the two, not unwilling, flew
between earth and starry heaven.
sentences.i: and the pair flew, not unwilling, between earth and starry heaven.
sentences.n: τὼ ‘the two’, ἀέκοντε ‘unwilling’ and πετέσθην ‘flew’ are all duals, the Greek number for a pair (the two horses). οὐκ ἀέκοντε ‘not unwilling’ means eager. μεσσηγύς ‘between’ takes the genitives γαίης (Ionic -ης) τε καὶ οὐρανοῦ ἀστερόεντος ‘of earth and of starry heaven’.

sentences.t:
ὅσσον δ’ ἠεροειδὲς ἀνὴρ ἴδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
ἥμενος ἐν σκοπιῇ, λεύσσων ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον,
sentences.tr:
hosson d’ ēeroeides anēr iden ophthalmoisin
hēmenos en skopiēi, leussōn epi oinopa ponton,
sentences.l:
And as much of the misty-looking distance as a man sees with his eyes,
sitting on a lookout, gazing over the wine-faced open-sea,
sentences.i: As much of the misty-looking distance as a man sees with his eyes, sitting on a lookout and gazing over the sea that has the look of wine,
sentences.n: A simile of distance: ὅσσον ‘as much as’ here is picked up by τόσσον ‘so far’ in the next line. ἠεροειδές ‘misty-looking’ is a neuter adjective used as a noun, ‘the hazy expanse’, and ἴδεν is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω (= εἶδεν) in a general statement. ἥμενος ‘sitting’ and λεύσσων ‘gazing’ are participles, ἐν σκοπιῇ ‘on a lookout’. οἴνοπα is the stock epithet of the sea, ‘wine-faced’, from οἶνος ‘wine’ and the root of ὄψ ‘face, look’.

sentences.t: τόσσον ἐπιθρῴσκουσι θεῶν ὑψηχέες ἵπποι.
sentences.tr: tosson epithrōiskousi theōn hypsēchees hippoi.
sentences.l: so far leap the high-sounding horses of the gods.
sentences.i: just so far do the high-sounding horses of the gods leap.
sentences.n: This is the main clause of the simile: each leap of the gods’ horses carries as far as a man sees from his lookout. τόσσον is ‘so far’, and ἐπιθρῴσκουσι is the present of ἐπιθρῴσκω ‘leap on, bound’. ὑψηχέες ‘high-sounding’ is built on ὕψι ‘on high’ + ἠχέω ‘sound’; the sense, perhaps of neighing, is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Τροίην ἷξον ποταμώ τε ῥέοντε,
ἧχι ῥοὰς Σιμόεις συμβάλλετον ἠδὲ Σκάμανδρος,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē Troiēn hixon potamō te rheonte,
hēchi rhoas Simoeis symballeton ēde Skamandros,
sentences.l:
But when now they came to Troy and to the two flowing rivers,
where the Simois and the Scamander join their streams,
sentences.i: But when they came to Troy and the two flowing rivers, where the Simois and the Scamander join their streams,
sentences.n: ἷξον is ‘they came’, the aorist of ἵκω, with Τροίην as the place reached. ποταμώ and ῥέοντε are duals, ‘the two rivers’ and ‘flowing’, and ἧχι is ‘where’. The two rivers of the Trojan plain are Σιμόεις (the Simois) and Σκάμανδρος (the Scamander); συμβάλλετον is a dual, ‘the two join’, and ῥοάς are their ‘streams’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἵππους ἔστησε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη
λύσασ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, περὶ δ’ ἠέρα πουλὺν ἔχευε·
sentences.tr:
enth’ hippous estēse thea leukōlenos Hērē
lysas’ ex ocheōn, peri d’ ēera poulyn echeue·
sentences.l:
there she stopped the horses, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
having unyoked them from the chariot, and poured much mist around;
sentences.i: there white-armed Hera, the goddess, stopped the horses, unyoked them from the chariot, and poured a great mist all around;
sentences.n: ἔστησε is ‘she stopped’ (transitive), and λύσασ’ the elided aorist participle ‘having unyoked’; ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘from the chariot’ (plural for one car). περὶ … ἔχευε is ‘poured around’, split by tmesis, and ἠέρα πουλύν is ‘much mist’, with the epic πουλύς (= πολύς). The object round which it is poured is not named.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ ἀμβροσίην Σιμόεις ἀνέτειλε νέμεσθαι.
sentences.tr: toisin d’ ambrosiēn Simoeis aneteile nemesthai.
sentences.l: and for them the Simois made ambrosia spring up to graze on.
sentences.i: and for them the Simois made ambrosia spring up to feed on.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν ‘for them’ means the horses. Σιμόεις, the river, is the subject, and ἀνέτειλε is the aorist of ἀνατέλλω used of causing to rise, ‘made spring up’. ἀμβροσίη ‘ambrosia’ is the food of the gods, here given to their horses, and νέμεσθαι ‘to graze on’ is a middle infinitive of purpose.

sentences.t:
αἳ δὲ βάτην τρήρωσι πελειάσιν ἴθμαθ’ ὁμοῖαι
ἀνδράσιν Ἀργείοισιν ἀλεξέμεναι μεμαυῖαι·
sentences.tr:
hai de batēn trērōsi peleiasin ithmath’ homoiai
andrasin Argeioisin alexemenai memauiai·
sentences.l:
And the two went, like timorous doves in their gait,
to defend the Argive men, eager;
sentences.i: And the two went, in their gait like timorous doves, eager to defend the Argive men;
sentences.n: αἳ δὲ ‘and they’ is a plural pronoun with the dual verb βάτην ‘the two went’; Homer mixes the numbers freely. τρήρωσι ‘timorous’ is the epithet of doves (πελειάσιν); ἴθμαθ’ is ‘in their gait’, an accusative of respect, and ὁμοῖαι ‘like’ agrees with αἳ. ἀλεξέμεναι is an epic infinitive ‘to defend’, with the dative ἀνδράσιν Ἀργείοισιν ‘the Argive men’, and μεμαυῖαι ‘eager’ is the feminine participle of μέμονα.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκανον ὅθι πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι
ἕστασαν ἀμφὶ βίην Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο
εἰλόμενοι λείουσιν ἐοικότες ὠμοφάγοισιν
ἢ συσὶ κάπροισιν, τῶν τε σθένος οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ hikanon hothi pleistoi kai aristoi
hestasan amphi biēn Diomēdeos hippodamoio
eilomenoi leiousin eoikotes ōmophagoisin
ē sysi kaproisin, tōn te sthenos ouk alapadnon,
sentences.l:
But when they came to where the most and the best
stood around the might of Diomedes, horse-taming,
crowded together, like raw-eating lions
or wild boars, whose strength is not feeble,
sentences.i: But when they came to the place where the greatest number and the best stood around the might of Diomedes, tamer of horses, pressed close together, like lions that eat raw flesh, or wild boars, whose strength is not feeble,
sentences.n: ἵκανον is ‘they came’, and ὅθι ‘where’ opens the clause. πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι is ‘the most numerous and the best’, and ἕστασαν is the pluperfect used as an imperfect, ‘were standing’. βίην Διομήδεος ‘the might of Diomedes’ stands for Diomedes himself, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘horse-taming’ is the epic genitive in -οιο. εἰλόμενοι ‘crowded together’ describes the men, and ἐοικότες + the dative means ‘like’; ὠμοφάγοισιν is ‘raw-eating’ (ὠμός ‘raw’ + φαγεῖν ‘eat’), συσὶ κάπροισιν ‘wild boars’ (σῦς and κάπρος, two words for the boar set side by side), and τῶν τε σθένος οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν ‘whose strength is not feeble’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα στᾶσ’ ἤϋσε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη
Στέντορι εἰσαμένη μεγαλήτορι χαλκεοφώνῳ,
ὃς τόσον αὐδήσασχ’ ὅσον ἄλλοι πεντήκοντα·
sentences.tr:
entha stas’ ēÿse thea leukōlenos Hērē
Stentori eisamenē megalētori chalkeophōnōi,
hos toson audēsasch’ hoson alloi pentēkonta·
sentences.i: there white-armed Hera, the goddess, took her stand and shouted, making herself like great-spirited Stentor of the bronze voice, who could shout as loud as fifty other men;
sentences.n: στᾶσ’ is the elided aorist participle of ἵστημι (intransitive), ‘having taken her stand’, and ἤϋσε is ‘shouted’. εἰσαμένη is the aorist participle of εἴδομαι, ‘having made herself like’, with the dative Στέντορι; μεγαλήτορι ‘great-spirited’ and χαλκεοφώνῳ ‘bronze-voiced’ are his epithets. In ὃς τόσον αὐδήσασχ’ ὅσον ἄλλοι πεντήκοντα the form αὐδήσασχ’ is printed so; it looks like the aorist participle of αὐδάω ‘speak aloud’, but the final χ’ is not explained. The sense, ‘called out as much as fifty others’, is not in doubt.

sentences.t: αἰδὼς Ἀργεῖοι κάκ’ ἐλέγχεα εἶδος ἀγητοί·
sentences.tr: aidōs Argeioi kak’ elenchea eidos agētoi·
sentences.l: “Shame, Argives, base disgraces, admirable in form!
sentences.i: “Shame, Argives, you base disgraces, admirable in form!
sentences.n: Hera, in Stentor’s voice, shouts at the Argives. αἰδώς is ‘shame’, used as an exclamation, and Ἀργεῖοι is the address. κάκ’ ἐλέγχεα is ‘base disgraces’ (κακά, ἔλεγχος ‘reproach, disgrace’), and εἶδος ἀγητοί is ‘admirable in form’: εἶδος is an accusative of respect, and ἀγητός ‘admirable’ is the adjective. The taunt is that their looks are fine and their conduct is not.
sentences.mark: Hera, as Stentor, shames the Argives

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν ἐς πόλεμον πωλέσκετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
οὐδέ ποτε Τρῶες πρὸ πυλάων Δαρδανιάων
οἴχνεσκον·
sentences.tr:
ophra men es polemon pōlesketo dios Achilleus,
oude pote Trōes pro pylaōn Dardaniaōn
oichneskon·
sentences.i: As long as heavenly Achilles used to go to the war, the Trojans never used to go out in front of the Dardanian gates;
sentences.n: ὄφρα μὲν … ‘as long as’ is followed by two iterative imperfects, πωλέσκετο ‘used to go to and fro’ and οἴχνεσκον ‘used to go about’; the suffix -σκ- marks repeated action. δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘heavenly Achilles’. πρὸ πυλάων Δαρδανιάων is ‘in front of the Dardanian gates’, the gates of Troy (Δαρδανίαι is the adjective from Dardanus, the Trojans’ ancestor), and οὐδέ ποτε is ‘never’.

sentences.t: κείνου γὰρ ἐδείδισαν ὄβριμον ἔγχος·
sentences.tr: keinou gar edeidisan obrimon enchos·
sentences.l: for that man’s mighty spear they feared;
sentences.i: for they were afraid of his mighty spear;
sentences.n: κείνου is the epic form of ἐκείνου ‘of that man’, with the emphasis on Achilles, and it goes with ἔγχος ‘spear’. ἐδείδισαν is ‘they feared’ (from δείδω, with a reduplicated stem), and ὄβριμον ‘mighty’ is the house word for ὄβριμος.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ ἑκὰς πόλιος κοίλῃς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ μάχονται.
sentences.tr: nyn de hekas polios koilēis epi nēusi machontai.
sentences.l: but now far from the city, by the hollow ships, they fight.”
sentences.i: but now they fight far from the city, at the hollow ships.”
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ turns from the past to the present. ἑκὰς πόλιος is ‘far from the city’ (ἑκάς takes the genitive, and πόλιος is the epic genitive of πόλις), and κοίλῃς ἐπὶ νηυσί is ‘by the hollow ships’, with the epic feminine dative plural κοίλῃς (= κοίλαις) and νηυσί (= ναυσί). The point of the taunt is that the Trojans fight at the Argive ships only because Achilles is out of the fight.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipous’ otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, she urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ is ‘so having spoken’ (εἰποῦσ’ is the elided aorist participle, feminine). ὄτρυνε is ‘urged on’, an aorist without the augment, and μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου is ‘the might and the heart of each man’; μένος is fighting strength, θυμός the spirit that drives a man. The line is the same as one already published, with the participle in the feminine, and its English is kept.

sentences.t: Τυδεΐδῃ δ’ ἐπόρουσε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: Tydeïdēi d’ eporouse thea glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: And upon Tydeus’-son rushed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena;
sentences.i: and the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, came rushing to the son of Tydeus;
sentences.n: Τυδεΐδῃ is the dative of Τυδεΐδης ‘Tydeus’-son’, a patronymic standing for Diomedes. ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush upon’, which takes the dative; here the rush is a friendly one. Ἀθήνη has her stock epithet γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’, as at 719.

sentences.t:
εὗρε δὲ τόν γε ἄνακτα παρ’ ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν
ἕλκος ἀναψύχοντα τό μιν βάλε Πάνδαρος ἰῷ.
sentences.tr:
heure de ton ge anakta par’ hippoisin kai ochesphin
helkos anapsychonta to min bale Pandaros iōi.
sentences.l:
and she found that lord by his horses and chariot
cooling the wound which Pandarus hit him with, with an arrow.
sentences.i: She found the lord by his horses and chariot, cooling the wound that Pandarus had given him with an arrow.
sentences.n: εὗρε is ‘found’, and τόν γε ἄνακτα ‘that lord’ is Diomedes, with γε adding a little emphasis. παρ’ ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν is ‘by his horses and chariot’ (ὄχεσφιν is the epic dative in -φιν). ἀναψύχοντα is the present participle of ἀναψύχω ‘cool off, air’, and ἕλκος ‘wound’ is its object; τό ‘which’ is the relative, and βάλε is ‘hit’. ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’ (not ἰός ‘poison’), ‘with an arrow’.

sentences.t:
ἱδρὼς γάρ μιν ἔτειρεν ὑπὸ πλατέος τελαμῶνος
ἀσπίδος εὐκύκλου·
sentences.tr:
hidrōs gar min eteiren hypo plateos telamōnos
aspidos eukyklou·
sentences.l:
For sweat was wearing him down under the broad strap
of the shield, well-rounded;
sentences.i: For the sweat was wearing him down under the broad strap of his well-rounded shield;
sentences.n: ἱδρώς ‘sweat’ is the subject, and ἔτειρεν is the imperfect ‘was wearing down’ of τείρω, with μιν ‘him’. ὑπὸ πλατέος τελαμῶνος is ‘under the broad strap’, the belt that carries the shield on the shoulder. εὐκύκλου is built on εὖ ‘well’ + κύκλος ‘circle’, hence ‘well-rounded’; ἀσπίδος is the genitive ‘of the shield’.

sentences.t:
τῷ τείρετο, κάμνε δὲ χεῖρα,
ἂν δ’ ἴσχων τελαμῶνα κελαινεφὲς αἷμ’ ἀπομόργνυ.
sentences.tr:
tōi teireto, kamne de cheira,
an d’ ischōn telamōna kelainephes haim’ apomorgny.
sentences.l:
by it he was worn down, and he grew weary in the arm,
and holding up the strap he was wiping away the dark-clouded blood.
sentences.i: by it he was worn down, and his arm grew weary; and, holding up the strap, he wiped away the blood, dark as a cloud.
sentences.n: τῷ τείρετο is ‘by this he was worn down’ (the passive of τείρω), with τῷ the dative of the sweat or the strap, which the Greek leaves open; κάμνε δὲ χεῖρα is ‘and he grew weary in the arm’ (χείρ is ‘hand’ or ‘arm’), χεῖρα being an accusative of respect. ἂν δ’ … ἴσχων is ‘holding up’ (tmesis), with τελαμῶνα as its object. κελαινεφὲς αἷμα is ‘dark-clouded blood’, an epithet usually of Zeus; ἀπομόργνυ is the imperfect of ἀπομόργνυμι ‘wipe away’, without the augment.

sentences.t: ἱππείου δὲ θεὰ ζυγοῦ ἥψατο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: hippeiou de thea zygou hēpsato phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: And the goddess touched the yoke of the horses and spoke:
sentences.i: The goddess laid her hand on the yoke of his horses and spoke:
sentences.n: ἱππείου ζυγοῦ is ‘the yoke of the horses’, with the adjective ἵππειος ‘of horses’ and the verb ἥψατο ‘touched’ taking the genitive. φώνησέν τε is ‘and she spoke’, the aorist of φωνέω with the enclitic τε.

sentences.t: ἦ ὀλίγον οἷ παῖδα ἐοικότα γείνατο Τυδεύς.
sentences.tr: ē oligon hoi paida eoikota geinato Tydeus.
sentences.l: “Truly a child little like himself Tydeus begot.
sentences.i: “Truly Tydeus fathered a son little like himself.
sentences.n: Athena opens with a taunt. ἦ is ‘truly’, and ὀλίγον ἐοικότα is ‘little like’, with ὀλίγον adverbial and ἐοικότα the perfect participle of ἔοικα, agreeing with παῖδα ‘child’. οἷ is the dative of the reflexive, ‘to himself’, and γείνατο is the aorist middle of γείνομαι, used of a father, ‘begot’; Τυδεύς, held to the end, is the subject, and the child is Diomedes.

sentences.t: Τυδεύς τοι μικρὸς μὲν ἔην δέμας, ἀλλὰ μαχητής·
sentences.tr: Tydeus toi mikros men eēn demas, alla machētēs·
sentences.l: Tydeus, I tell you, was small in build, but a fighter;
sentences.i: Tydeus, I tell you, was small in build, but a fighter;
sentences.n: τοι is the enclitic ‘I tell you’, and μικρὸς μὲν ἔην δέμας is ‘was small in build’, with δέμας an accusative of respect and ἔην the epic imperfect of εἰμί. The μέν is answered by ἀλλά ‘but’, and μαχητής ‘fighter’ is the predicate.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ὅτε πέρ μιν ἐγὼ πολεμίζειν οὐκ εἴασκον
οὐδ’ ἐκπαιφάσσειν, ὅτε τ’ ἤλυθε νόσφιν Ἀχαιῶν
ἄγγελος ἐς Θήβας πολέας μετὰ Καδμείωνας·
sentences.tr:
kai rh’ hote per min egō polemizein ouk eiaskon
oud’ ekpaiphassein, hote t’ ēlythe nosphin Achaiōn
angelos es Thēbas poleas meta Kadmeiōnas·
sentences.i: Even when I would not let him fight or dash out, when he came away from the Achaeans as a messenger to Thebes, among the many Cadmeans,
sentences.n: Athena recalls Tydeus’ errand to Thebes, told by Agamemnon at 4.384–390. καί ῥ’ ὅτε πέρ is ‘even when’, and εἴασκον is the iterative imperfect of ἐάω, ‘I would not let’, with the infinitives πολεμίζειν ‘fight’ and ἐκπαιφάσσειν ‘dash out’ (a rare word, from παιφάσσω ‘dart about’; its sense is not certain). ὅτε τ’ ἤλυθε is ‘when he came’ (ἤλυθε = ἦλθε), with νόσφιν Ἀχαιῶν ‘away from the Achaeans’. ἄγγελος is ‘as a messenger’, and πολέας … Καδμείωνας ‘the many Cadmeans’ are the Thebans; the main verb comes in the next line.

sentences.t: δαίνυσθαί μιν ἄνωγον ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἕκηλον·
sentences.tr: dainysthai min anōgon eni megaroisin hekēlon·
sentences.l: I bade him feast at ease in the halls;
sentences.i: I bade him feast at ease in the halls;
sentences.n: ἄνωγον is ‘I bade’, past tense of ἄνωγα, and δαίνυσθαί the infinitive ‘to feast’. ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν is ‘in the halls’ (the epic forms of ἐν and the dative plural), and ἕκηλον ‘at ease’ agrees with μιν ‘him’. This finishes the sentence begun at 802: even when she held him back, she told him to stay at the feast.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ θυμὸν ἔχων ὃν καρτερὸν ὡς τὸ πάρος περ
κούρους Καδμείων προκαλίζετο, πάντα δ’ ἐνίκα
ῥηϊδίως·
sentences.tr:
autar ho thymon echōn hon karteron hōs to paros per
kourous Kadmeiōn prokalizeto, panta d’ enika
rhēïdiōs·
sentences.i: but he, with his own strong spirit as before, kept challenging the young men of the Cadmeans, and won at everything easily;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ is ‘but he’ (Tydeus), and θυμὸν ἔχων ὃν καρτερὸν ‘keeping his own strong spirit’ has the possessive ὅς ‘his own’; ὡς τὸ πάρος περ is ‘as before’. κούρους Καδμείων is ‘the young men of the Cadmeans’, and προκαλίζετο is the imperfect middle ‘kept challenging’. πάντα δ’ ἐνίκα … ῥηϊδίως is ‘and won at everything easily’, with ῥηϊδίως the epic form of ῥᾳδίως. The lines follow 4.389–390, and the English of the repeated words is kept.

sentences.t: τοίη οἱ ἐγὼν ἐπιτάρροθος ἦα.
sentences.tr: toiē hoi egōn epitarrothos ēa.
sentences.l: such a helper to him was I.
sentences.i: Such a helper was I to him.
sentences.n: τοίη ‘such’ is feminine, as the speaker is, and οἱ is ‘to him’. ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ ‘I’, ἦα the epic imperfect 1 sg. of εἰμί (= ἦν), and ἐπιτάρροθος a ‘helper’, a rare word of unclear formation. At 4.390 the same is said of Athena in the third person (τοίη οἱ ἐπίρροθος ἦεν Ἀθήνη), and the English follows it.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγὼ παρά θ’ ἵσταμαι ἠδὲ φυλάσσω,
καί σε προφρονέως κέλομαι Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
soi d’ ētoi men egō para th’ histamai ēde phylassō,
kai se prophroneōs kelomai Trōessi machesthai·
sentences.l:
And you, for my part, I stand beside you and guard you,
and readily I bid you fight the Trojans;
sentences.i: As for you, I stand by you and guard you, and I readily bid you fight the Trojans;
sentences.n: σοὶ … παρά θ’ ἵσταμαι is ‘I stand beside you’, with παρά split from its verb by tmesis and governing the dative σοί, and ἠδὲ φυλάσσω ‘and I guard’. ἤτοι μὲν ἐγώ is ‘I for my part’, set against what Tydeus did. κέλομαι is ‘I bid’, with σε and the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’, which takes the dative Τρώεσσι ‘the Trojans’; προφρονέως is ‘readily’, with a ready mind.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά σευ ἢ κάματος πολυᾶϊξ γυῖα δέδυκεν
ἤ νύ σέ που δέος ἴσχει ἀκήριον·
sentences.tr:
alla seu ē kamatos polyaïx guia dedyken
ē ny se pou deos ischei akērion·
sentences.l:
but either much-darting weariness has sunk into your limbs,
or else fear, I suppose, now holds you, spiritless;
sentences.i: but either a weariness that darts upon you again and again has sunk into your limbs, or else some spiritless fear, I suppose, has hold of you;
sentences.n: Athena gives two possible causes for his holding back. ἢ … ἤ is ‘either … or’; σευ γυῖα is ‘your limbs’ (σευ the epic genitive of σύ), and δέδυκεν is the perfect of δύω ‘has sunk into’. πολυᾶϊξ ‘much-darting’ is built on πολυ- ‘much’ and a root meaning ‘dart’ (as in ἀΐσσω); the exact force is not known. νύ ‘now’ and που ‘I suppose’ soften the second guess. ἀκήριον ‘spiritless’ is taken from κῆρ ‘heart’; the word is rare and its sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
οὐ σύ γ’ ἔπειτα
Τυδέος ἔκγονός ἐσσι δαΐφρονος Οἰνεΐδαο.
sentences.tr:
ou sy g’ epeita
Tydeos ekgonos essi daïphronos Oineïdao.
sentences.l:
you are not then
the offspring of Tydeus, wise-minded, the son of Oeneus.”
sentences.i: then you are not the offspring of wise-hearted Tydeus, the son of Oeneus.”
sentences.n: οὐ σύ γ’ ἔπειτα is ‘then you are not’, the conclusion Athena draws, with ἐσσι the epic ‘you are’ and ἔκγονος ‘offspring’. δαΐφρονος ‘wise-minded’ (the sense is disputed) agrees with Τυδέος, and Οἰνεΐδαο ‘son of Oeneus’, an epic patronymic in -αο, stands beside it. Athena ends her speech here without waiting for an answer, and Diomedes replies in the next part.
